title: The greatest era
subtitle: The case that Ottoman Rhodes, 1522 to 1912, was the best the town ever had

chapters.title: The case, and how to judge it
chapters.text:
Rhodes town has had many golden ages on offer. The one on the postcards is ancient: the Colossus, the fleet, the schools of rhetoric. The one on the walking tours is medieval: the Knights Hospitaller, their hospital, their Street of the Knights. The Ottoman centuries between 1522 and 1912 usually appear as the part where nothing much happened, or where things went downhill.
This essay argues the opposite. It claims that the Ottoman period was the greatest era in the history of Rhodes town. That is advocacy, and I will not pretend otherwise. But it is advocacy that has to survive its own counter-arguments, so the terms need fixing before the case begins.
"Greatest" can mean glory: the most famous monuments, the biggest victories, the widest influence. By that measure ancient Rhodes wins easily, and I will say so plainly in chapter seven. But glory is a thin way to judge a place where people actually lived. The town is a place first, and a monument second.
So here are four criteria. First, security and continuity: how long did ordinary people live in the same houses, in the same trades, without a siege, a sack or a change of master? Second, plurality: how many communities lived together in the town, and how were they treated by the standards of their own age, not ours? Third, stewardship: what did the era build, and what did it keep standing for later generations? Fourth, standing: how much did Rhodes matter to the wider world that governed it?
On the first three, I will argue, the Ottoman era has no serious rival in the town's history. On the fourth it is respectable but not outstanding, and I will not claim more. I will also not claim that Ottoman Rhodes was rich. The evidence for its economy is thin and mostly points to a modest provincial port.
Nor will I claim that it was fair. Christians were barred from sleeping inside the walls for most of the period. Non-Muslims paid a special tax and lived under a legal hierarchy. There was violence in 1821, there was slavery, and there was a catastrophic explosion in 1856. Chapter eight sets these out without softening them.
What remains, after the weighing, is a claim that is narrower than "the Ottomans were wonderful" and harder to dismiss. For nearly four centuries a fortress town that had been fought over for most of its history was simply left to be lived in. Three peoples made homes there, and one of them, the Sephardic Jews, built something that outlasted the empire by only a generation. The old town you can walk today is, to a degree most visitors do not suspect, what that long peace left behind.

chapters.title: A surrender that was mostly kept
chapters.text:
The siege of 1522 is told elsewhere in this tour, and from the Ottoman side in its own piece. Here a few sentences will do. Suleiman's army landed in late June 1522, the Hospitaller defenders under Grand Master Philippe de Villiers de l'Isle-Adam held out through the summer and autumn, and in December, with the walls breached and the garrison exhausted, they asked for terms. Dates for the last days vary by source, but the capitulation was agreed between about 20 and 22 December.
What matters for this essay is what the terms were, and how far they held. The Knights were given twelve days to leave with their weapons, valuables and religious relics. Islanders who wanted to go could do so within three years. Those who stayed were to be free of Ottoman taxation for five years. And no church was to be desecrated or turned into a mosque.
On 1 January 1523 the Knights sailed, and some 4,000 Rhodians sailed with them. A later tradition says that Suleiman, watching the old Grand Master leave, was moved to say he regretted forcing a brave man from his home. I cannot trace that remark to a source from the time, so treat it as a later story rather than a record.
The church clause did not last the month. The great conventual church of St John, at the top of what is now the Street of the Knights, became the town's main mosque, known in Ottoman sources as the Cami-i Kebir, the Great Mosque. The first Friday prayer was held there on 20 January 1523. That is a broken promise and I will not dress it up. Other churches became mosques over the following decades, and the Suleymaniye, the first great mosque of the conquest, rose on a church site.
Even so, compare what happened next with what a sack would have meant. There was no massacre of the population and no burning of the town. The fortress was not slighted, and the walls that had cost the Order two centuries of work were left standing. The Italian scholar Rossi, writing in 1927, observed that the Turks did not touch the fortress, the inns of the langues, the buildings of the Castellania or the great hospital, and left almost intact the coats of arms, gateways and inscriptions. That is why you can still read "D'Auvargne" and "DAMBOYSE MDXII" on stone in the old town.
The new rulers also kept the town's basic structure of trade and craft. The bazaar axis, today's Sokratous street, stayed the commercial spine, and the Ottomans filled the Knights' old compound at the top of the town with their own officials: the castle warden, the steward and the aghas, as the traveller Evliya Çelebi describes it in the seventeenth century.
A fair summary is that the surrender terms were honoured in their main purpose, which was to spare lives and property, and broken in their religious clause. That mixed record is itself a theme of the next three and a half centuries.

chapters.title: Four centuries without a siege
chapters.text:
The first claim of the case is the simplest: Ottoman Rhodes was quiet for a very long time.
Start with the town's earlier history. In the ancient world Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged it in 305 and 304 BC, and it held. In 88 BC Mithridates tried and failed. In 43 BC Cassius took the city and sacked it. In the seventh century Arab forces raided and for a time held the island, and in the centuries before the Knights it passed between Byzantine officials, local lords and Italian adventurers, a rough sequence of at least half a dozen changes of master, though I have not reconstructed every one. Then the Hospitallers arrived, in 1309 or 1310 depending on how one counts, and their Rhodes was a frontier fortress state. It was attacked by Mamluk fleets in 1440 and 1444, besieged by Mehmed II in 1480, and besieged again in 1522. It also took an earthquake on 3 May 1481, about a year after the siege, that damaged houses and fortifications, and a plague between 1498 and 1500.
Now the years after the Ottomans. In May 1912 Italian troops landed and fought a campaign of about two weeks across the island before the Ottoman garrison surrendered near Psinthos, on 16 May by most accounts. In September 1943 Italians and Germans fought each other for the island after Italy's armistice. In 1944 Allied bombs fell on the old town and destroyed parts of it, a famine struck the civilians in 1944 and 1945, and in July 1944 the Jewish community was deported. Within about thirty-five years the town went from Italian conquest to German occupation to British administration to union with Greece.
Between those two clusters stands a stretch of 390 years in which, as far as I can find, the town of Rhodes was never besieged, never stormed and never sacked. I say "as far as I can find" because I have not read a complete chronicle of every raid and naval scare in the eastern Mediterranean over four centuries, and a reader who knows of an exception should weigh it. The travellers' accounts I have read, such as that of Henry Tozer, who landed in April 1886, describe a garrison town and a bazaar, not a city living in fear of attack.
Why? Partly geography and empire. After 1522 Rhodes sat inside the Ottoman maritime world rather than on a land frontier. Venetian Crete lay nearby until 1669, and the Knights had moved to Malta, where their corsairs still raided Ottoman shipping, so the danger was real; I simply know of no attack that reached the town. One famous incident shows it. In 1748, Hungarian, Georgian and Maltese slaves aboard the galley Lupa rose against their masters and sailed to Malta, taking more than 150 Ottomans prisoner, among them Mustafa, the former pasha of Rhodes. Rhodes was exposed to the sea war, but it was never the target.
I should be careful about what this proves. A long peace is not the same as a golden age, and a town can be peaceful and poor. Roman and early Byzantine Rhodes also enjoyed long quiet stretches, and taken together those centuries were longer than the Ottoman era, though under a dozen dynasties and with an Arab occupation. What I claim is narrower. No single regime held Rhodes town for longer, and none gave ordinary families so long a run without the sudden catastrophes that marked the town's earlier and later history.
That is a real good. Houses stay in families, trades pass from father to son, and a street can acquire a name. The 1831 Ottoman census lists twenty-three Muslim neighbourhoods inside the walls, named for a mosque or a prayer-house, such as the neighbourhood of the bootmaker Ali Agha or of the judge. A town does not generate that kind of fine-grained, trade-and-congregation address system in a decade. It does so over generations.

chapters.title: Three peoples, one town
chapters.text:
The second claim is about plurality. Ottoman Rhodes was a town where Muslims, Orthodox Greeks and Jews all lived, worshipped, traded and judged their own affairs, under one government, for centuries.
I should explain how it was organised, with a caution. Guidebooks say the Ottomans ran a "millet system" of self-governing communities. The substance is right for Rhodes: the Orthodox Metropolitan judged Greek family and inheritance cases, the rabbis ran the Jewish courts, and the kadi's court heard criminal and commercial matters for everyone. But historians such as Benjamin Braude have shown that the tidy three-millet scheme is largely a nineteenth-century codification. Say "communities with their own courts", not "the millet system".
The geography of that arrangement was this. Muslims and Jews lived inside the walls. Greeks lived in suburbs outside, the marasia, eight of them in the Greek church tradition, each named for its parish: Metropolis, Agia Anastasia, Agios Nikolaos and so on. A mid-nineteenth-century estimate gives about 5,500 Muslims and 1,000 Jews inside the walled town, and about 5,000 Greeks in the suburbs and 47 villages. These are period estimates, not a census, but they show the scale: a town of several thousand, mixed.
The Greek Orthodox Church was in a better position under the Ottomans than it had been under the Knights. Under the Order the Greek clergy had answered to a Latin archbishop. After 1522 the Latin hierarchy left with the Knights, and the Orthodox Metropolitan, seated in the Metropolis suburb, led and judged his community with no Latin superior over him. Greek churches in the marasia could be built only after the mid-eighteenth century, when permission was given, so this was no equality. But the Orthodox hierarchy was back, and for a majority of the island's people, who spoke Greek and prayed in Greek, that was not nothing.
The Jewish story is where the case is strongest, and I want to tell it carefully.
Rhodes had a Jewish community from antiquity. When Benjamin of Tudela visited in the 1160s he counted about 400 Jews in Rhodes. They were Romaniote Jews, Greek-speaking, with their own liturgy. Under the Hospitallers things went badly. After the 1480 siege, according to the chronicler Elijah Capsali, Grand Master d'Aubusson ordered the Jews to convert; some accepted baptism and some chose death. In 1502 he decreed that they leave Rhodes, sailing only to Nice, and Wikipedia's account of d'Aubusson says he expelled adult Jews and forcibly baptised their children. The scale and enforcement are debated and the decree may not have been fully carried out before he died in 1503. The shape is not debated. The Order also held thousands of Jewish captives, taken at sea, as labour on its fortifications, and it is said that in 1522 they helped the Turks.
The date matters for everything that follows. In 1492 Spain expelled its Jews, and in 1496 and 1497 Portugal forced the survivors to convert or leave. The Ottoman sultan Bayezid II welcomed the refugees into his empire, and Sephardic communities grew across the eastern Mediterranean. In 1523, the year after the conquest, the Ottomans resettled 150 Jewish families from Thessaloniki in Rhodes. A 1906 Jewish encyclopedia adds that Suleiman gave them twenty years free of tax and a free house for each family. I treat the free house as a tradition reported by a reference work, not a document anyone has shown.
What grew from that start is remarkable. The new community absorbed the older Romaniote one and made Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish language, the speech of the Juderia. Kahal Shalom was founded in 1577 and is the oldest synagogue in Greece, with a central bimah and two Torah arks; one source adds a renovation in 1593. The community later built or rebuilt other synagogues, including the Midrash in 1865 with money from the Camondo banking family. It ran its own courts, charities and, from the nineteenth century, schools. Around 1905 the Jewish Encyclopedia put the Jewish population of the town at about 4,000 and said the commerce of the island was largely in Jewish hands, from the Alhadeff bank to the boatmen at the harbour.
Compare the standard of the age. Between 1290 and 1497 Jews were expelled from England, France, Spain and Portugal, and in 1502 from Rhodes by the Knights. Here a state not only allowed them to stay but resettled them, and left them in the walled town while sending Greeks out. The traveller Charles Fellows in 1841 noted that Jews were locked each night within their own quarters of the town, and Tozer in 1886 wrote that the Jewish quarter held many of the handsomest old dwellings, and that Jews were allowed inside the walls because the Turks regarded them as too timid to be dangerous. That is a Victorian gloss, and a patronising one, but it records the structural fact that the Jews were a trusted, if subordinate, community.
The worst episode confirms this rather than contradicting it. In February 1840 a Greek Orthodox boy disappeared and the Greek community accused the Jews of ritual murder. The Ottoman governor, Yusuf Pasha, urged on by European vice-consuls, had a Jewish man beaten with five hundred blows and blockaded the Jewish quarter for twelve days. That is the ugly face of a plural town. Yet the Ottoman centre then intervened. A commission released the prisoners and acquitted them in July, found the affair "the product of hatred", and dismissed the governor for using torture that the reform edict of 1839 had forbidden. In November 1840 a sultanic firman declared the charge pure calumny. The local majority, the consuls and the provincial governor all failed. The imperial court protected the minority.
Now the comparison after 1912. Italy's racial laws of 1938 drove more than 2,000 of the island's roughly 4,000 Jews to emigrate. On 23 July 1944 the German command marched 1,673 Jews to the harbour. They were shipped to Piraeus, and from Haidari near Athens deported to Auschwitz, where they arrived on 16 August. About 150 came back. A refuge that had lasted four centuries ended in a single week.

chapters.title: The town they kept
chapters.text:
The third claim, and the one most likely to surprise a visitor, is about preservation. The medieval town of Rhodes survives, to a large degree, because the Ottomans kept it.
Consider what happened in other fortress cities. Rulers who take a town often rebuild it in their own image, and Rhodes could easily have lost its Gothic stones. Instead the Ottomans adapted. The walls, which the Order had spent two centuries strengthening, remained a garrison fortress under Ottoman officers. The inns of the langues became houses and offices. The Hospital, the Castellania, the gates and the street pattern stayed. Churches received a minaret and a mihrab, and their walls were plastered. The Italian architectural historian Balducci, cited in a 2022 Turkish study, records that most of the small neighbourhood mosques were Byzantine or Hospitaller churches treated in just this way.
That reuse is partly why UNESCO's World Heritage evaluation says that building after 1523 combined local forms, from the meeting of two worlds, with decorative elements of Ottoman origin. What you see in the alleys today is a Hospitaller stone shell with Ottoman additions: enclosed timber balconies, called sachnisi in Greek, from the Turkish şahnişin, hung over the lane so that women could watch the street through lattice. Courtyards were laid in black-and-white pebble mosaic, a craft that Rhodes shared across faiths, so that a Hospitaller floor, a Turkish courtyard and the synagogue at Kahal Shalom use the same technique.
Now the awkward part. Ottoman stewardship had limits. The Wikipedia article on the town says the decline of the empire resulted in general neglect of the buildings, made worse by earthquakes. The Grand Master's Palace was no longer a palace, and the Ottomans used its vaults to hold convicts. And in 1856 the explosion I discuss in chapter eight destroyed the church of St John and much of the Palace.
But look at the alternative. In the Italian period, from 1912 to 1943, the town was substantially rebuilt. The Italians restored the Knights' buildings, and they also demolished Ottoman ones. One summary of their plan says they preserved what remained from the Knights' period and destroyed all Ottoman buildings in the area they worked on. The celebrated Ottoman baths were demolished in 1912 and 1913, if the Human Rights Without Frontiers report is right. Between 1937 and 1940 the architect Vittorio Mesturino rebuilt the Palace of the Grand Master from the ruin left by the explosion, as a holiday residence for King Victor Emmanuel III and Mussolini, to a standard criticised for lack of historical accuracy. The Medusa mosaic inside came from Kos. Mussolini never came.
So when a visitor admires the Knights' town, they are admiring three layers. There is a Hospitaller core, there is an Ottoman layer that held it in being through four centuries of use, and there is an Italian layer of the 1920s and 1930s that cleaned some of it up, tore some of it down and invented some of it. The Italian town was a stage set. The Ottoman town was a lived one, and the stones survived the living.
This is a matter of degree, not an absolute. The Order's builders deserve their credit, and the Italians' restorers saved much that might otherwise have gone. But the sheer fact of survival, the tombs of the grand masters aside, depends on 390 years in which nobody bombarded, razed or modernised the place. You can call that neglect or you can call it stewardship, and the two are not far apart. A town that is neglected in the right ways keeps its character.

chapters.title: What they built
chapters.text:
Preservation is half of stewardship. The other half is addition, and Ottoman Rhodes added a good deal that is still standing.
The mosques come first. The Ibrahim Pasha Mosque on Platonos Square is dated to 947 AH, which is 1540 or 1541, and is the oldest mosque on the island. Other dates are quoted, among them 1531 and a tradition that it was ordered by Suleiman's grand vizier Pargalı Ibrahim before his execution in 1536, so say the 1530s or 1540s. It is the only mosque inside the walls still in regular use, and was formally licensed for worship only in 2019. The Rejep Pasha Mosque on Dorieos Square, completed in 1588, is usually called the finest, with a single dome on a sixteen-sided drum, Iznik tile panels and ancient columns reused from earlier buildings. The Murad Reis Mosque, completed around 1623, stands in a walled Ottoman cemetery behind Mandraki, where Lawrence Durrell lived in the gatekeeper's lodge in 1945 and found the marble gravestones with their flowing Arabic inscriptions a not ineffective monument to that lost epoch.
The Suleymaniye Mosque on Sokratous street is the one everyone sees. Tradition makes it the first mosque of the conquest, though Ottoman sources date it to 1541 with an imaret and a hammam. The present building is a rebuild of 1808. Its octagonal fountain stands on eight columns taken from older buildings.
Then there are the secular buildings, which are more interesting. The Yeni Hammam on Arionos Square is first mentioned in an imperial decree of 1558, and the women's wing was added under Mustafa III in the 1760s. It is the only Ottoman bath still standing in Rhodes. A bath mattered more than it sounds: for an Ottoman woman it was the one public building she could use as of right. It has been closed for restoration for years, so you can look at the domes and little more.
Across the lane from the Suleymaniye stands the Hafiz Ahmed Agha Library, which I think is the best single argument for this chapter. Hafiz Ahmed, born around 1740 in the village of Asgourou, rose to chief equerry to the sultans Abdulhamid I and Selim III. He set up his foundation in Istanbul on 26 February 1792 and the library opened in Rhodes in 1793. The charter required teachers to give free Arabic and Quran lessons to the children of the Muslim community. It holds about 1,260 manuscripts, in Ottoman Turkish, Arabic and Persian; counts vary between 1,256 and 1,265, and the figure at the founding is given variously as 828 or nearly 2,000. The foundation says that it has been run by the founder's descendants, now in the seventh generation, without interruption, and calls itself the only private Ottoman-era foundation of its kind outside Turkey. That is the foundation's claim, and I have no means of testing it. A foundation that has survived Italian rule, the Greek junta and the twenty-first century is at least a remarkable fact.
His son Ahmed Fethi Pasha, marshal of the arsenal in Istanbul, added to the corner. In 1850 to 1852 he built the clock tower, the Roloi, and a house for the timekeeper who calculated prayer times from the sun, and in 1853 a junior high school. The clock came from Edward Prior and Company of London. A Muslim endowment was buying a London clock to give a mixed town one shared time.
How much more was there? The Ottoman foundations register for 1885 counts 44 mosques on Rhodes, four dervish lodges, three madrasas, a library, a primary school, a middle school, 50 water fountains and 20 Muslim cemeteries, all tied to pious endowments. Read it as the Ottoman welfare state: worship, hospitality, schooling, drinking water and burial, paid for from the rents of endowed shops and orchards rather than by taxes. The fountains are the humblest part of it. In Islamic law building a public fountain earned merit for the soul, so the town gradually filled with them.
I should keep the claim in proportion. These are good provincial buildings, not masterpieces to rank with Istanbul's, and several are closed or damaged today. The Hospitaller and ancient layers contain finer things. The argument is not that Ottoman architecture of Rhodes outclasses the Knights' work but that the Ottomans kept adding, over centuries, in a town they could easily have used only as a barracks.

chapters.title: Rhodes in the Ottoman world
chapters.text:
The fourth criterion, standing, is where the case is weakest, so I will lay out the evidence and not inflate it.
Administratively, Rhodes was first the seat of a beylerbey, a provincial governor. In 1546 it was reduced to a sanjak, a sub-province, of the Eyalet of the Archipelago, which was the province of the Kapudan Pasha, the grand admiral. It seems to have become the admiral's seat in the late seventeenth century. In 1849 it became a pasha-sanjak, and in the later nineteenth century it was a candidate capital of the Archipelago province, moving between Rhodes and other towns, back in Rhodes by 1888. In 1912 the sanjak covered Rhodes, Kos, Symi, Kastellorizo, Karpathos and Kasos. All of this is a good, functional posting, though not an imperial centre.
The more telling evidence is who was sent there. Rhodes was an island of exile, as it had been under Rome, when Tiberius spent a few years there. Ottoman statesmen who fell from favour were sent to Rhodes. The former grand vizier Rami Mehmed Pasha, after governing Cyprus and Egypt, was exiled to Rhodes in 1706 and died there. The satirical poet Haşmet, whose real name was Mehmed, was exiled for lampooning grandees, spent his last years on the island and died there in 1768 or 1769, with his grave in the Murad Reis complex. TDV's encyclopedia dates his exile to Rhodes to the 1760s, and the details vary. In the 1880s the reforming writer Namık Kemal, one of the Young Ottomans, served as district governor of Rhodes, after Lesbos and before Chios, a posting that was a polite exile for a man Abdulhamid II distrusted.
Being a place of exile is not a distinction, but it is a clue to rank. You send an enemy to a place that is far, quiet and safe. Ottoman Rhodes was all three, and it hosted, over nearly two centuries, a former grand vizier, a satirical poet and a patriotic playwright and journalist. The Murad Reis cemetery holds the corsair-admiral who gave it its name, who died in 1609 by most accounts. Rhodes took part in the world of the Ottoman navy even when it did not lead it.
What about the economy? This is the weakest part of the case, and I will not overclaim. Historians have largely abandoned the simple notion of a continuous Ottoman decline from the sixteenth century. The empire adapted to new trade routes, its provincial elites grew in power, and in the nineteenth century Ottoman ports such as İzmir expanded sharply with European trade. But I cannot show that Rhodes shared that growth. Nearby Symi grew rich on sponges in the mid-nineteenth century. Rhodes town, by contrast, appears in travellers' accounts as a quiet garrison town, with about 6,000 people inside the walls in 1815, when William Turner counted about 5,000 Turks and 1,000 Jews, and a Greek population in the suburbs and villages. The 1831 census lists about 1,970 registered Muslims, probably men only, in the twenty-three neighbourhoods. The Wikipedia article on the city speaks of general neglect. I found no reliable figures for the town's population across the whole period, only these snapshots.
So the honest summary is that Ottoman Rhodes was stable and unremarkable economically, and the case for it rests on what stability allowed, not on prosperity. That is a smaller claim, and I think a defensible one.

chapters.title: The rival golden ages
chapters.text:
Now the obvious objection. Any reader who loves the Colossus will say that Hellenistic Rhodes was a greater thing, and in the terms most people mean by "great", they are right.
Consider the case on its own terms. In 408 or 407 BC the three old cities of the island merged into a new city at the north end. For more than two centuries after that Rhodes was an independent state with a fleet that policed the seas, a democratic-aristocratic constitution that ancient writers admired, and a diplomacy that kept the Hellenistic kings at arm's length. When Demetrius laid siege to it in 305 and 304 BC it held out, and the Colossus, a giant bronze Helios, was raised afterwards to celebrate the victory. It stood for only part of a century before an earthquake brought it down, usually dated to 226 BC, though recent research reopens the date. The city also sent teachers to the world. The rhetorician Apollonius Molon taught Cicero and Caesar. Pliny credits Rhodian sculptors with the Laocoon group. Rhodian maritime customs, notably the rule on sharing losses when cargo is thrown overboard, entered Roman law, though historians dispute how much of a formal Rhodian code ever existed. Amphora stamps show a trade network that reached across the Mediterranean.
On the fourth criterion, standing in the world, there is no contest. Hellenistic Rhodes was a power. Ottoman Rhodes was a posting.
But Hellenistic Rhodes does less well on the other three. It was never at peace for long. It was besieged, it lost its independence by degrees after 167 BC when Rome made Delos a free port and cut its revenues, and Cassius sacked it in 43 BC. Like every ancient city it relied on slave labour. The state's structure was a hierarchy of citizens, resident foreigners and slaves; the famous Rhodian clubs, the koina, included many foreigners, but political power belonged to citizens. By the standards of its day it was an enlightened place, and I admire it. By the standard of how many different people lived securely together, it was a smaller and more exclusive city than Ottoman Rhodes.
The period also ended, in effect, in the second century BC. The peak of independent greatness lasted perhaps a century and a half. The Ottoman era lasted 390 years.
That brings me to the Knights. The Hospitaller town is the one the tour spends most time on, and its achievements are real: the hospital, the walls, the inns, the Street of the Knights. But it was a frontier garrison run by a religious order, funded in part by war and piracy at sea, and for most of its time it lived expecting the next siege. It had four classes of subject, and Greek Orthodox Rhodians lived under a Latin archbishop. It expelled or forcibly baptised its Jews and used captives as fortification labour. It lasted just over two centuries and ended when it lost the island.
In defence of the Knights, much of what visitors admire is theirs. The walls that made the town were built under the Order. The point is not that the Order was contemptible but that its great creation was a fortress, and a fortress is made to be attacked. In the end it was.
So here is the fair comparison. If the question is "which era made Rhodes most famous", the answer is the Hellenistic one. If the question is "which era built the strongest walls", it is the Hospitaller one. If the question is "in which era did the most people live the longest in the same town, with the most communities side by side, and leave the most intact town behind", then it is the Ottoman. I think the third question is the better one for a place where you can walk the streets today. But I recognise that a reader who disagrees is not being foolish. The criteria are a choice.

chapters.title: The ledger against
chapters.text:
Everything above has to be set against the harm done. I will take the main counts in turn.
The first is the sunset rule. In 1886 H. F. Tozer, an Oxford geographer, wrote that the gates of the city were closed at night and no Christians were allowed to remain within the walls, so that Greeks who kept shops there had to leave at sunset. He added that until about forty years earlier all Christians had to leave on Fridays before noon, on the theory that the city would one day be retaken on a Friday when the faithful were at prayer. So three and a half centuries after the conquest a Greek shopkeeper on Sokratous street still walked home through the gate every evening. One advocacy report says that Christians caught inside after dark were liable to be beheaded, but I found no primary confirmation, and it should be treated as tradition. The rule itself is solid, and it is a real injury. It treated the island's Orthodox majority as visitors in the capital of their own island.
The second is legal inequality. Non-Muslims paid the cizye, a poll tax, in lieu of military service, until the reform edict of 1856 proclaimed civil equality. Churches in the marasia could be built only from the mid-eighteenth century, with permission. The Orthodox and the Jews were protected, but as subordinate communities. The Ottoman state's tolerance was a hierarchy: a good hierarchy by the standards of its age, but a hierarchy.
The third is violence. On this point I have to be careful, because I could not find a detailed account for Rhodes. During the Greek War of Independence Rhodes and Kos did not join the uprising, although many Rhodians belonged to the secret Filiki Etaireia and fled to join the rebels. Wikipedia, drawing on the historian William St Clair, says that Greek populations on Rhodes and Kos suffered massacres in the wave of reprisals that spread across the Aegean in 1821. I could not confirm details such as numbers or names. The 1824 destruction of Kasos, which belonged to the sanjak of Rhodes, was carried out by Ottoman and Egyptian forces and killed or enslaved a large part of its population. It did not occur in the town, but it was done in the name of the same administration. The honest position is that Rhodes was not a site of atrocity on the scale of Chios or Kasos, but it was touched by them.
The fourth is slavery. The Ottoman Empire had slavery, and Rhodes was part of it. The Pasha Mustafa's household held slaves, including a man from Tripoli whom his father had promised to free, and galley slaves rowed Ottoman ships, as the Lupa revolt shows. But the Knights held slaves too, including thousands of Jewish captives, and ancient Rhodes depended on slaves. No era in the town's history is clean of it, and it is not a reason to prefer another one.
The fifth is the decline narrative. I said earlier that most historians now reject the idea of a simple Ottoman decline, and that is true of the empire as a whole. For Rhodes in particular the evidence shows a stagnant town with neglected buildings. A reader who concludes that Ottoman Rhodes was poor and slow has the sources behind them. My claim is that poor and slow can coexist with secure and plural, and that a town can be the second without the first.
The sixth is the explosion. On 6 November 1856 lightning struck gunpowder stored in the cellars of the bell tower of the church of St John, which by then was the Great Mosque. At least 200 people were killed, the church was destroyed and much of the Grand Master's Palace with it. Six Grand Masters had been buried in that church, and their tombs were lost. Tozer reports that the Turkish authorities at the time of the explosion were ignorant of the powder's existence, and Wikipedia says it was possibly stored there since 1522. A garrison sat for three centuries on top of a magazine nobody had inventoried. That is a failure of administration, and the single greatest loss of Hospitaller heritage in the town's history.
I would add one thing about the 1522 clause on churches, which the Ottomans broke. No honest account can defend that. But a broken promise about churches is not a massacre, and the fortress was kept.
Weigh all this and you get the following. The Ottoman era was not just. It was safe, and it was long, and it contained injustices that were embedded in the system and not accidental. The case for it as the greatest era does not need those facts to be false. It needs only that the alternatives were worse on the criteria that matter, and that a place can be great without being good.

chapters.title: After 1912, and what is left
chapters.text:
The case closes with the end of the era, because endings are a kind of test.
In May 1912 Italy took Rhodes during the Italo-Turkish War, and the Ottoman garrison surrendered. The Italians stayed, and the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 confirmed their possession of the Dodecanese. Because the islands were under Italian rule, their Muslim community was not included in the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey, which sent Muslims out of mainland Greece and Orthodox Christians out of Turkey. That is why Rhodes still has a Muslim community today. After the islands joined Greece, with the ceremony in Rhodes on 7 March 1948, the community shrank sharply. Estimates today run from about 2,000 to 4,000, depending on who is counting. Many emigrated to Turkey, in waves after 1967 and 1974. The last Turkish-language school, in the Suleymaniye Medrese at the top of the Street of the Knights, was closed in 1972 by the Greek junta, though the ministry dates the last Turkish-language schools to 1991. An anthropologist who studied the community reports that for decades official guides were told not to mention the Ottoman past.
The mosques and Muslim cemeteries of the island are held by a state-supervised foundation, the Vakouf of Rhodes. Rejep Pasha, Murad Reis and the Suleymaniye are closed or in poor repair, and the Ibrahim Pasha Mosque is the one that is open. Greece has restored some of them recently, and there is a small revival of interest, so the picture is not simply one of loss.
The Jewish ending was far worse. Of about 4,000 Rhodian Jews in 1930, over 2,000 left after the 1938 laws, and almost all the rest were deported in 1944. About forty Jews live on Rhodes today, and the community now exists mostly as a diaspora, in Rhodesli congregations in Seattle, Los Angeles and Africa, that comes back each July. The Turkish consul Selahattin Ülkümen, who in 1944 told the German commander that under Turkish law all citizens are equal and saved around forty-two to fifty people, was a diplomat of the Turkish Republic, not of the empire. I do not claim continuity of states. I note only that his argument, equality before the law, echoes the ruling of the Ottoman commission of 1840.
There is one more honest piece of the balance sheet. For most of the island's people, who were Greek and Orthodox, the 1948 union with Greece is a great moment, and the Dodecanese still hold its anniversary. A Greek Rhodian can reasonably say that the best moment in the town's history is the one when it came home, and nothing in this essay refutes that. It is a different criterion: national self-determination, in place of the four I have used.
So the verdict is conditional, as honest verdicts are. If you weigh glory and fame, the Hellenistic city wins. If you weigh fortress craft, it is the Knights. If you weigh national self-rule, it is the modern Greek town. If you weigh how long ordinary people of several faiths lived in security in the same streets, how much they built and kept, and what the town they left behind looks like today, then the Ottoman centuries have the best claim.
Perhaps the fairest test is the one you can carry out yourself. Walk up Sokratous street past the Suleymaniye, turn into the courtyard of the library, then go down to Platonos Square and stand outside the one mosque still in use. Then walk east to Kahal Shalom and the Square of the Jewish Martyrs. In an hour you will have crossed three communities' worth of town, all within the walls, most of it built or kept during those 390 years. The town you are looking at is mostly Ottoman. It is worth knowing that.

sources:
Evidence and sources

This essay draws on the project's own research notes (checked against sources in September 2026) and on a small number of additional checks. Where sources conflict I have said so in the text. Much of the ancient and medieval background is standard and comes from general reference works. The Ottoman material is thinner and more dependent on a few specialist studies, which are named below.

Travellers and primary voices

  • H. F. Tozer, The Islands of the Aegean (1890): eyewitness account of Rhodes in April 1886, including the sunset rule for Christians, the Jewish quarter, the ignorance of the powder store, and the closed walls.
  • Charles Fellows (1841) and William Turner (1815): early nineteenth-century travellers, as quoted in secondary sources, for the Jewish quarter and the walled-town population.
  • Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname, book IX: the seventeenth-century Ottoman traveller, as cited by modern scholars, on the Knights' quarter under Ottoman use.
  • Benjamin of Tudela: twelfth-century Jewish traveller who counted about 400 Jews in Rhodes.

Modern scholarship and reference

  • F. Evliyaoğlu, "Osmanlı Döneminde Rodos Kentindeki Camiler ve Mahalleler Üzerine Bir İnceleme", Art-Sanat 17 (2022): the 1831 census mahalles, mosque conversions, first Friday prayer, Ottoman use of the Collachium.
  • Benjamin Braude on the millet system, as summarised in reference works: why the three-millet scheme is a later codification.
  • Marc D. Angel, The Jews of Rhodes (1978): standard history of the community; I did not have the book to hand and cite it as the principal work, not for specific claims.
  • Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) and Jewish Virtual Library: the Hospitaller decrees, the 1523 resettlement, the community around 1905.
  • Rhodes Jewish Museum and Rhodes Holocaust documentation: Kahal Shalom, daily life, the 1944 deportation figures.
  • Frankel, The Damascus Affair, as summarised in reference works: the 1840 Rhodes blood libel and its reversal.
  • Human Rights Without Frontiers (2015) and PACE Doc. 12526 (2011): the Muslim community after 1947, the schools, the foundation; advocacy sources, used with care.
  • Fethi Pasha Foundation and Hafiz Ahmed Agha Foundation sites: the library and clock tower, in the foundation's own words.
  • Wikipedia articles on the Sanjak of Rhodes, the Church of St John of the Collachium, the Murat Reis Mosque, the Palace of the Grand Master and the Italian occupation, as routes to their cited sources.

The least well-sourced parts of the essay are the economy and population of Rhodes between 1600 and 1900, the events of 1821 on Rhodes itself, and slavery in Ottoman Rhodes, where I found only scattered evidence.
